sections.h2: Is gain on a New Jersey house sale taxable?
sections.html:
Yes. The state counts gain on a house as income, figured by the federal method, so whatever is taxable on the federal return is taxable here as well. The Division's guide routes the gain through the same return as your other income, for the year of the sale (NJ Division of Taxation home guide).

Gain is the amount realized minus your adjusted basis, and basis begins with your cost. If you inherited the house, the IRS sends you to Publication 551 for the basis rules. The IRS does not allow a deduction for a loss on a home you lived in.

The state's top bracket matters for large gains. New Jersey raised its Gross Income Tax rate to 10.75 percent on income above $1 million beginning with tax year 2020, and a big sale can push a seller into that bracket in a single year.

sections.h2: Who can exclude the gain on a New Jersey home sale?
sections.html:
Owners of a main home may shelter $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 filing jointly, once they pass the tests below. New Jersey follows the federal exclusion, and it applies whether you stay in the state or move away.

  • Ownership: you held title for at least two of the five years that end on the closing date.
  • Use: you made it your main home for at least two years inside that same window.
  • Additional home: no gain from another home was excluded in the two years before this sale.
  • A joint filing couple reaches $500,000 only if both pass the use test, and a couple where just one spouse qualifies is held to $250,000.

Sellers who miss the two year mark because of a job change, health problem or unforeseen event may claim a reduced exclusion. A Form 1099-S obliges you to report the sale to the IRS even when the whole gain is excluded (IRS Topic 701). Rental properties, second homes and vacation homes do not count as a principal residence.

sections.h2: What changes if the gain is above the exclusion?
sections.html:
The excess is a capital gain, and federal rates depend on how long you held the house. A house held for a year or less produces short term gain, taxed as ordinary income. A longer hold earns lower rates, and for tax years that began in 2025 the rate was 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on taxable income (IRS Topic 409).

The IRS lists a few extras that sellers of residential property sometimes run into. The IRS also lists a 25 percent ceiling on unrecaptured section 1250 gain, and those with significant investment income may face the net investment income tax. Federal reporting goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D.

New Jersey adds its own filing steps. Residents report the gain on Schedule B of the NJ-1040 as Net Gains or Income From Disposition of Property. Nonresidents use Part I of the NJ-1040-NR. If the sale produced a loss, the state form takes a zero on that line.

sections.h2: Do I owe New Jersey tax at the closing table?
sections.html:
Only a nonresident seller pays at closing, although all sellers file a GIT/REP form to record the deed. A seller who keeps a New Jersey residence files form GIT/REP-3 at closing, which exempts the estimated payment. The tax on any gain is then settled with the NJ-1040 the following filing season.

A New Jersey resident who sells and moves out of state counts as a nonresident for this sale. The nonresident figure is 2 percent of the consideration or 8.97 percent of the net gain, sent before or at closing, and a seller's assurance on GIT/REP-3 can waive it. The check is made out to the State of New Jersey, Division of Taxation, and travels with the paperwork to the settlement agent.

sections.h2: Which GIT/REP exemptions are common, and who signs?
sections.html:
Whoever must sign the deed signs the form, which may be the seller or an authorized representative with a power of attorney or letter of authority. Each owner files, married and civil union couples count as one owner, and an estate or trust files a single form that can carry several trustee or executor signatures.

  • The seller is a New Jersey resident.
  • Total consideration is $1,000 or less.
  • The seller is a business entity.
  • The seller is a nonresident claiming the principal residence exclusion.

The only sales that skip the form are sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales. A county clerk can still reject a deed for reasons outside the Division's control. The Division suggests printing its instructions, highlighting the relevant passage and showing it to the clerk before escalating (GIT/REP FAQs).

sections.h2: How do I get back an overpaid estimated payment?
sections.html:
A nonresident seller can file Form A-3128 after closing to claim an early refund of an overpayment. The Division wants proof such as the settlement statement or closing disclosure. The form does not replace the NJ-1040-NR, which must still be filed for the year the property sold, and the final refund comes out of that return.

Because the 2 percent and 8.97 percent figures are estimates, a seller who took a small gain or a loss often overpays. Keep the closing disclosure, the deed, and records of improvements together so the return is easy to prepare.

sections.h2: What records should a New Jersey seller keep for the return?
sections.html:
Keep the paperwork that proves your basis and the closing numbers, because the gain is figured on the return and not at the table. A nonresident who sold must file the NJ-1040-NR for the year the property was sold, and the closing payment is listed on the estimated payment line.

  • The settlement statement or closing disclosure from the purchase and from the sale.
  • Receipts for capital improvements. The Division notes that New Jersey does not allow certain federal deductions such as mortgage interest or capital improvements on the NJ-1040, so these receipts matter for basis and not for a deduction.
  • The signed GIT/REP form and any payment receipt.
  • For an inherited house, the paperwork showing its value when the owner died. IRS Publication 551 covers inherited basis.

Estates and trusts complete one GIT/REP form, and it can carry signatures from more than one executor or trustee. Ask the estate's tax preparer how the sale is reported on the estate's own return.

faqs.q: Does New Jersey have its own capital gains tax for a home sale?
faqs.a: No separate tax exists. The state taxes the gain through its Gross Income Tax and follows the federal calculation, so a federally taxable amount is also taxable here.

faqs.q: What is the exclusion limit for spouses who sell together?
faqs.a: Spouses filing jointly can exclude up to $500,000 once the tests are met. When only one of them qualifies, the cap falls to $250,000.

faqs.q: Do I pay an estimated tax at closing if I stay in New Jersey?
faqs.a: No. A resident who remains in the state submits form GIT/REP-3 and pays any income tax when filing the NJ-1040.

faqs.q: What if I sell and relocate out of New Jersey?
faqs.a: For this sale, you count as a nonresident. The estimated deposit applies unless an exemption fits, and a nonresident return follows for the year of the sale.

faqs.q: Which return reports the sale for a nonresident?
faqs.a: Form NJ-1040-NR, Part I, as Net Gains or Income From Disposition of Property, with any closing payment listed as an estimated payment, not as withholding.
